newsitem.title: USA: New product lets your brain drive the PC.
newsitem.headline: New product lets your brain drive the PC.

text.p: Like something out of science fiction, computer users can command their machines just by thinking, using a new technology launched Wednesday by a California company.

Ron Gordon, president of The Other 90% Technologies Inc., said the small, privately held company was introducing its MindDrive product in entertainment software that was being sold at more than 400 computer retail outlets.

"Today we're going to take a first step in a new technology that could be a great benefit for all of us," said Gordon, known for introducing Atari Corp.'s pioneer video game, Pong, in the early 1970s.
"It's a great way to use your computer and a great way to use your mind," he told reporters.
The device relies on a sensor placed around a computer user's finger. The sensor plugs into a black box containing specialised software, which in turn connects to the back of a personal computer.

The product uses The Other 90%'s patented filtering technology to decipher electrical signals given off by human skin and arising from thoughts. Those signals alone can, for example, guide a digital skier down a computer-depicted slalom course.
MindDrive inevitably prompts comparisons with countless science-fiction movies and books where a character flies or moves objects simply through thought.
The Defence Department and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration have worked on vastly more expensive devices to help pilots fly supersonic aircraft.

However, Gordon said the San Rafael, Calif.-based company was starting out with entertainment software since the technology, which took seven years to develop, cannot yet stand up to more demanding tasks.
The MindDrive hardware and software package retails for about $149.95. The 10 initial games and other software products are priced from $24.95 to $39.95, for use only on IBM-compatible machines.
The Other 90% takes its name from physicist Albert Einstein's observation that humans use only about 10 percent of their brain power.
The company is also in a joint venture with The Walt Disney Co.'s Miramax studio to develop short films whose plot and outcome are controlled by viewers' thoughts.
Miramax's president of marketing, Mark Gill, said such a movie could make its debut at the start of 1997 on the Internet.
Gordon said his company was exploring other potential alliances and uses for the technology.

The National Easter Seals Society, the non-profit organisation for the disabled, also has expressed interest in the product. It could provide entertainment and perhaps revolutionary help for people who cannot use their limbs.
"In its present state I don't think it could drive a wheelchair, but it's not too far off," said society spokesman Roger Wellman.
The Other 90% has about 65 employees, Gordon said. The company's capitalisation is about $5 million and he predicted about $40 million in sales of the MindDrive product through January 1997.
Gordon said he might take the company public "after a few profitable quarters" but would never sell it.
